Initially, all the above-mentioned seven Petitions were admitted separately. However, since they raise many common issues for consideration, the Petitions have been subsequently clubbed together for a comprehensive adjudication, ensuring consistency in decision-making and procedural efficiency. Also, the Pleadings in these matters have also been completed. However, in view of the APTEL’s DVC Judgment, as upheld by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in SC Order, TPCL moved an affidavit in these matters stating that, in terms of the ratio laid down in the above decisions, these matters require to be mandatorily referred to the arbitration by the Commission. Subsequently, both sides were permitted to file their respective submissions on the above aspect and were also heard extensively, as noted below. 5. Learned senior counsel for the Respondent, TPCL, submitted that the issues involved in the batch Petitions do not have any bearing on tariff and supply of power and thus, such issues are to be considered as ‘non-tariff’ issues and should be mandatorily referred to resolution by arbitration in light of the DVC Judgment of the APTEL which was also upheld by the Hon’ble Supreme Court. Learned senior counsel for the Petitioners, PSPCL, HPPC and GUVNL in Petition Nos. 85/MP/2022, 123/MP/2022 and 107/MP/2023, respectively, submitted that the matters would not be required to be referred to Arbitration. The Commission, after considering the submissions of the parties, permitted the parties to file the affidavits bringing on record the subsequent developments in the matter in light of the DVC judgment as well as the SC Order. **Issue No.1: Whether the dispute involved in this batch of Petitions is connected with the** **_‘regulation of tariff’_ of TPCL** **_?_ In other words, whether the dispute, as explained by the DVC Judgment, is a ‘tariff’ dispute or a ‘nontariff’ dispute?** **Issue No.1: Whether the dispute involved in this batch of Petitions is connected with the** **_‘regulation of tariff’_ of TPCL** **_?_ In other words, whether the** 17. The Procurers have primarily contended that the Commission has the necessary power to adjudicate upon the disputes involved in the batch of Petitions, and they are not required to be mandatorily referred to an arbitration in terms of the DVC Judgment as averred by TPCL. In support of the above contention, the Procurers have mainly raised the following grounds: - (b) The disputes raised by the procurers for adjudication in the present batch of Petitions squarely fall within the scope of regulatory functions having an impact on tariff directly and/or indirectly, and since the DVC Judgment itself categorises such disputes as “tariff disputes”, they are not wholly non-tariff disputes, which can be referred to the arbitration. - (a) The disputes raised by the Procurers in the present batch of the Petitions are in the nature of “contractual breach” and the prayers sought by them seek relief through (i) specific performance, and (ii) damages/ exemplary damages along with cost(s) allegedly owing to the expensive purchase of alternate power. followed and party cannot seek to reply on the general provisions (Section 79) by raising a collective dispute petition filed under Section 79(1)(b) and (f) of the Act. Also, the Procurer’s action against WRLDC gives rise to a separate cause of action, which can be bifurcated for the purpose of referring the principal dispute between the Procurers and TPCL to arbitration and with the secondary /independent relief against WRLDC to be governed by action, if any, under Sections 28(3)(a) and 28(5) of the 42. We have considered the submissions made by the parties. The Procurers have submitted that their claims in the Petition cannot be split to refer some to arbitration. As already settled by the Hon’ble Supreme Court, there cannot be a splitting of the cause of action in order to determine the issue of arbitration. Whereas, TPCL has submitted that the Procurers’ dispute qua WRLDC must be treated independently, being governed by Section 29 of the Act. and not Section 79 of the Act. The Procurers’ action against WRLDC gives rise to a separate cause of action, which can be bifurcated for the purpose of referring the principal dispute between the Procurers and TPCL to arbitration and secondary/ independent relief against WRLDC to be governed by the action, if any, under Section 28 of the Act. (i) The primary/principal dispute involved the Procurers and TPCL in this batch of Petitions does relate to tariff or regulation of tariff of the latter and such disputes, thus, do not fall within the ambit of adjudicatory jurisdiction of this Commission under Section 79(1)(f) read with Section 79(1)(b) of the Act. 49. Keeping in view the nature of disputes and the value involved in this batch of Petitions, the Commission finds it appropriate to refer the dispute(s) between the Procurers and TPCL as involved in this batch of the Petitions to a panel comprising three arbitrators as per Regulation 49(1)(b) of the COB Regulations, 2023. Accordingly, both sides, i.e., TPCL and Procurers, are to suggest the names of the Arbitrator in terms of the said Regulation within two weeks from the date of this order, and the third arbitrator shall be nominated based on the suggestion of both the nominated arbitrators.
